items.name: Andrej Karpathy
items.description: Explains neural networks, transformers, and LLMs with unusually clear engineering intuition
items.summary: Explains neural networks, transformers, and LLMs with unusually clear engineering intuition
items.body_html:
Overview

Builds and explains neural-network training from the tensor operations upward. The teaching and the code are the same artefact: nanoGPT and the from-scratch series let you follow a complete training loop rather than infer it from a framework's internals.

Why Follow

Useful when you want the mechanics of a transformer explained from the operations up rather than from the API surface, and when you want a training implementation small enough to read completely in an afternoon.

Notable Work

nanoGPT, a roughly 300-line GPT implementation that trains on Shakespeare and real checkpoints; the “Let's build GPT” and “Let's build the GPT Tokenizer” series; “A Recipe for Training Neural Networks”; the tokenizer and data-preparation tooling in minbpe and llm.c.

Channels

  • Primary profile
  • youtube
  • github

Resources

  • nanoGPT
  • minbpe — byte-level BPE tokenizer
  • llm.c — GPT-2 in C and CUDA

items.description: Popularizes practical AI education and structured learning paths
items.summary: Popularizes practical AI education and structured learning paths
items.body_html:
Overview

Teaches machine learning as an engineering discipline, organised into courses rather than papers. His influence is largely curricular: the DeepLearning.AI catalogue is the default onboarding path for ML across a lot of companies.

Why Follow

Useful for the framing that matters when you are teaching ML to an engineering organisation rather than to researchers, and for the clearest public treatment of structuring an ML project around measured error instead of intuition.

Notable Work

DeepLearning.AI and the Coursera machine-learning specialisation; Machine Learning Strategy, on error analysis and the ML project checklist; the AI Agentic Design announcement; “Generative AI for Everyone” as the executive-level entry point.

Channels

items.name: Arvind Narayanan
items.description: Writes critically about AI evaluation, policy, risks, and societal impact
items.summary: Writes critically about AI evaluation, policy, risks, and societal impact
items.body_html:
Overview

Writes about AI as an economics and measurement problem rather than a technique problem. The recurring argument is that capability claims, benchmark numbers and deployment reality are three different things, and that the gap between them is where most bad AI decisions are made.

Why Follow

Useful as a corrective when you are making decisions off benchmark and vendor numbers, and for the clearest public writing on why an eval is a diagnostic instrument rather than a scorecard.

Notable Work

“Evals are a tool, not a scorecard” and related essays on AI measurement; the cost, capital and infrastructure side of the LLM discourse; work on the practical economics of running models at scale.

Channels

  • Primary profile
  • website

Resources

  • Applied ML — essays and papers
  • Interconnected AI

Writes and speaks about the operational layer between a trained model and a shipped product: serving, inference cost, latency, and the engineering decisions that determine whether a model is viable in production.

Useful for applied ML systems decisions — what to serve, how to structure batch versus online inference, when a model is good enough to ship, and how inference cost changes the architecture you should pick.

Notable Work

Founded and runs Hugging Face, and argues publicly that training data is a public good whose licensing and accessibility decide who can build competitive models.

Why Follow

Useful for the open-data position specifically: if your work touches dataset provenance, licensing, or data access rather than model architecture, his is the clearest public argument for why that layer is a strategic decision.

Notable Work

Hugging Face as a company and platform; the Datasets and Transformers libraries; advocacy on open data and on AI's effect on research access.

Co-founded Anthropic and writes about capability, safety and compute, including the internal trade-offs a frontier lab actually weighs. The essays are unusually explicit about decisions usually left in internal documents.

items.name: François Chollet
items.description: Writes about abstraction, intelligence, benchmarks, and deep learning practice
items.summary: Writes about abstraction, intelligence, benchmarks, and deep learning practice
items.body_html:
Overview

Argues that intelligence is not a model-training outcome, and that benchmark progress has been conflated with capability. Built ARC-AGI to reward generalisation over memorisation, and designed Keras.

Why Follow

Useful for the strongest published dissent on the current approach, and for the reference point to bring when someone cites benchmark improvement as evidence of a capability jump.

Notable Work

“On the Measure of Intelligence” (the ARC paper); the ARC-AGI benchmark and its deliberately non-learnable task design; Keras's design and authorship; essays distinguishing skill-acquisition from general intelligence.

Channels

  • Primary profile
  • github
  • website

Resources

  • On the Measure of Intelligence
  • ARC-AGI benchmark
  • Keras

Overview

Argues publicly that autoregressive next-token prediction plus scale is not a path to the kind of understanding we want, and proposes a world-model alternative.

Why Follow

Useful as the most sustained technical dissent from inside the field, and for the concrete world-model research programme offered as an alternative rather than only a critique.

Notable Work

The convolutional and residual-architecture work; “A Path Towards Autonomous Machine Intelligence”; the JEPA line of self-supervised world-model research; the TVM compilation stack.
